description: We turn NASA data into tools people can trust. We build full data-to-decision systems: NASA/NOAA data pipelines, ML forecasts (Random Forest, LSTM) and AI assistants that explain science in plain language, checked against official sources (RAG + LangGraph). Our goal: put NASA Earth data in the hands of people who need it, like farmers facing heat, drought and floods. Looking for: web/front-end developer, designer/storyteller, climate or agriculture enthusiasts and curious learners.
summary: Sky-to-Soil is a web-based decision-support tool that helps farmers choose crop rotations that rebuild soil health and adapt to a changing climate. A farmer drops a pin on their field and sets their priorities: save water, build soil, lower climate risk, or stay close to familiar crops. Sky-to-Soil then combines 25 years of NASA POWER climate data, MODIS satellite vegetation history and local soil data with a crop knowledge base, and shows how this farm's climate has shifted. It scores [N] realistic two-year rotations on water fit, heat risk, soil health and soil suitability, and stress-tests them against a hotter, drier future. An AI agronomist then explains the best options in plain English or Urdu, and a rule-based fact check verifies every number it uses. Farmers get transparent, data-driven choices instead of guesswork.
details:
What it does Sky-to-Soil turns NASA Earth observations into crop-rotation advice that a farmer can understand and act on. In under two minutes, a farmer (or an extension officer helping them) gets:

  1. A climate shift report for their own field: how daytime and night-time temperature, hot days above 35 °C, seasonal rainfall and root-zone soil wetness changed between 2001–2012 and 2013–2025, with Mann-Kendall trend tests and Sen's slope.
  2. Field health from space: a multi-year MODIS NDVI vegetation history showing the field's cropping cycles.
  3. Ranked crop rotations: every realistic two-year, four-season rotation is scored 0–100 on water fit, heat risk, soil health, soil suitability and land use, weighted by the farmer's own priorities. The tool also shows the Pareto-optimal set and lets farmers compare two plans side by side.
  4. A climate stress test: each plan is re-scored under +1.5 °C and −15% rainfall to show which plans stay robust.
  5. An AI agronomist that explains the chosen plan in English or Urdu, answers questions about this farm, and cites its sources.
  6. A downloadable PDF farm plan to share with extension officers.

How it works

  • Backend (Python, FastAPI): async clients fetch NASA POWER daily data (temperature, rainfall, root-zone soil wetness, solar radiation, humidity, wind), MODIS MOD13Q1 NDVI through the ORNL DAAC web service, and ISRIC SoilGrids soil properties, with caching and graceful fallbacks. If SoilGrids is unavailable, users can pick a soil type from cited presets.
  • Science: reference evapotranspiration (FAO-56 Hargreaves and Penman-Monteith), crop water demand (ETc = Kc × ET0) against effective rainfall, heat-stress days during each crop's sensitive stage, and soil-health rules (legumes, crop-family breaks, diversity, residues).
  • Crop knowledge base: 14 crops (wheat, rice, maize, cotton, sugarcane, chickpea, lentil, mungbean, sorghum, pearl millet, mustard, potato, berseem clover, soybean) with cited FAO-based parameters.
  • AI agronomist (LangGraph + Groq, gpt-oss-120b): the model only sees a compact "facts" object computed by our science engine. A rule-based verifier (no AI) checks that every number matches the facts, that only real crops and sources are named, and that there are no guarantees. If a draft fails, the system rewrites it once; if it still fails, it falls back to a safe template. In our evaluation, [X]% of first drafts passed and 100% of delivered outputs passed the fact check.
  • Frontend (Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind, shadcn/ui, MapLibre, Recharts): a setup wizard, a dashboard, a rotation explorer, an agronomist panel, an English/Urdu interface with right-to-left support, and a mobile-friendly design.
  • Quality: [143] automated backend tests and a production build with no errors.

Benefits

  • Farm-specific: every number comes from this field's own NASA data, not regional averages.
  • Transparent: every score shows its parts and reasons, so farmers and extension officers can trust and question it.
  • Honest AI: the assistant explains but never invents numbers.
  • Accessible: plain language and Urdu support for smallholder farmers; it works for any location on Earth.

Our goals To help farmers move away from soil-depleting monocultures and water-hungry rotations toward diverse, legume-rich, climate-resilient plans, starting with Pakistan's Punjab and scalable worldwide.

Tools, languages and software Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, httpx, NumPy, pandas, pytest, LangGraph, Groq API, reportlab; TypeScript, Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, MapLibre GL, Recharts; hosted on Render (backend) and Vercel (frontend); GitHub.
